title: Microsoft Authenticator Flaw Let Rogue Android Apps Steal Work Account Tokens With No Permissions
excerpt: Enclave researchers found an app with zero permissions could impersonate Teams and have Authenticator hand over work-account tokens; Microsoft patched the flaw as CVE-2026-80097, CVSS 8.6, in version 6.2606.4246.
body:
• A flaw in Microsoft Authenticator for Android let an unprivileged app with zero permissions impersonate a Microsoft app such as Teams and receive that app's work-account tokens — no prompt, password or approval needed.
  • Microsoft patched the issue as CVE-2026-80097, rated CVSS 8.6, on September 8; all Authenticator for Android versions before 6.2606.4246 are affected.
  • In Enclave's tests the stolen tokens opened the victim's mailbox, files and calendar, and impersonating Authenticator itself could change sign-in methods and create or delete passkeys.
  • What to do: update Authenticator to 6.2606.4246 or later from the Google Play Store today if you use it for a work account on Android.

An app whose whole job is security trusted the identity its caller claimed, even though it knew who was actually calling. That is the finding Enclave researchers published on October 23 in a write-up titled AuthMask: a single exported activity in Microsoft Authenticator for Android handed out tokens for a signed-in work account to an app with no permissions at all, according to Enclave.

"We found that an unprivileged Android app with zero permissions could impersonate any installed Microsoft first-party app and have the Microsoft Authenticator broker hand it that app's tokens."

— Ofek Levin, Enclave researcher

How the attack worked

Authenticator exposes an activity called com.microsoft.identity.client.AccountChooserActivity, marked exported, which means any app on the device can launch it. The broker request it processed — package name, client ID, redirect URI, requested scopes and even the caller UID — all came from the calling app itself. Authenticator checked the redirect URI against the signature of the app being impersonated, but an attacker can read that signature from the Teams app already installed on the phone, so the check passed. The real calling app's identity, which Android makes available, was never used for a trust decision.

The setup needed only two things: Authenticator installed, and one work account signed into it. There was no user interaction beyond that.

What the tokens opened

With one work account signed in, Enclave's test app received tokens that could read and send email from the victim's mailbox, read and change files, calendar and SharePoint sites, and send Teams messages as the victim, according to Help Net Security. By pretending to be Authenticator itself, the app obtained permissions to change the account's sign-in methods, including creating and deleting passkeys — a way for an attacker to keep access even after the malicious app is removed.

The attack still required a malicious app to be installed on the device, which is why Microsoft classified it as a local elevation-of-privilege vulnerability. Once installed, though, the theft was silent: no prompt and no warning.

The fix and what to do

Enclave reported the flaw through responsible disclosure. Microsoft confirmed it and released a fix tracked as CVE-2026-80097, published September 8, 2026 and rated CVSS 8.6. Users should update Microsoft Authenticator from the Google Play Store and check they are on version 6.2606.4246 or later; IT teams managing company devices should enforce that minimum version through mobile device management, and everyone should be careful about sideloading apps from outside trusted stores.
